diagnostic_evidence.quote: Since the $\ell_i$ ($i>0$) are all independent, it follows that

issues.failure_explanation: The strong-induction argument assumes only that $r_n$ is independent of each $\ell_i$ separately (pairwise) and then concludes that $\ell_{n+1}=g(r_n,c_n)$ is independent of $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$. Pairwise independence of $r_n$ from each $\ell_i$ does not imply that $(r_n,c_n)$ is independent of the vector $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$, which is what the conclusion requires. Moreover, the induction step never shows that $r_{n+1}$ is independent of $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$ (only that $r_{n+1}$ is independent of $\ell_{n+1}$), so the hypothesis is not propagated. Statement (ii) asserts only pairwise independence, while Corollary cor:added-2 uses $\mathbb{E}[\prod\ell_i]=\prod\mathbb{E}[\ell_i]$, which needs mutual independence.

failure_location.quote: Assume that $r_n$ is independent from $\ell_i$ ($i=1,\dots,n$). The base case is validated by the computations above.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen the induction hypothesis to: $r_n$ is independent of the vector $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$. Since $c_n$ is independent of $(r_n,\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$, $(r_{n+1},\ell_{n+1})=(T(c_n,r_n),g(c_n,r_n))$ is independent of $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$; combined with part (i) this yields both the propagated hypothesis and mutual independence of $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_{n+1}$. State (ii) as mutual independence.
issues.overall_effect: As written, mutual independence of the $\ell_i$ (and hence $\mathbb{E}[L_n]=\mathbb{E}[\ell_1]^n$) is not established; the conclusions are true but their proof has a gap.
issues.title: Independence induction in Theorem thm - ind is incomplete (pairwise vs. joint/mutual independence; hypothesis not propagated)
issues.why_classification: A short, standard rewording of the induction (joint instead of pairwise independence) fully repairs the proof and preserves every stated conclusion and rate.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Since $\mathcal{T}(G_n)$ is a cumulative density function, it is clearly positive and bounded.
Let $\mathcal{T}: X \to Y$ be a positive linear operator preserving linear functions.
If $r_0$ does not have a point mass at $0$ or $1$ (that is, $\mathbb{P}[r_0=0]=\mathbb{P}[r_0=1]=0$) and if the cuts $c_n$ are not almost surely at 0 or 1, then
Let us make a brief digression from the main objective of this section to note that the conditions in \Cref{thm - root_conv} are optimal.

issues.failure_explanation: Positivity of a linear operator means $G\ge 0\Rightarrow \mathcal{T}G\ge 0$ for all $G$ in the domain. The paper only checks that $\mathcal{T}$ maps CDFs (nondecreasing $G$) to nonnegative functions. For non-monotone $G\ge0$ the integrand $G(tc)+G(t+(1-t)c)-G(c)$ can be negative: e.g. for $c=1/2$ a.s. and $G=\mathbf 1_{\{1/2\}}$, $(\mathcal{T}G)(t)=-1$ on $(0,1)$; for a Beta(2,2) cut density $f$, a narrow bump $G$ at $1/2$ gives $(\mathcal{T}G)(0.6)<0$ since $f(0.8\overline{3})/0.6<f(1/2)$. Hence Theorem thm - conv is applied outside its hypotheses. The conclusion is in fact false under the stated hypotheses: take $c_n=1/2$ a.s. (not a.s. 0 or 1) and $r_0=1/3$ (no mass at 0 or 1). Then $r_n$ alternates deterministically between $1/3$ and $2/3$, $G_n$ is a single step function, $\|\mathcal{T}^kG_0(t)-t\|\ge 2/3$ for all $k$, and the displayed bound (with $\varepsilon=\delta<1/3$) is violated for large $k$. Any deterministic cut $c_0\in(0,1)$ with a deterministic root is likewise a counterexample. The same example with $c=1/3$ a.s. and $r_0=1/2$ gives $\ell_n\in\{1/3,2/3\}$ deterministic, so $\mu_{\ell_n}\not\to 5/9$ and $\sigma^2_{\ell_n}=0\ne \tfrac{2}{9}\cdot\tfrac19$, falsifying Corollary cor - mean_variance_gen and the convergence claim of Theorem thm - pdf_general; the 'optimality of conditions' digression is also wrong.

failure_location.quote: and thus a positive linear operator from $B_\circ[0,1]$ to $B_\circ[0,1]$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must add hypotheses under which $\mathcal{T}$ is genuinely positive on $B_\circ[0,1]$ (for cut densities $f$ this is equivalent to $xf(x)$ nondecreasing and $(1-x)f(x)$ nonincreasing, which includes the uniform cut but excludes Beta(2,2), Bates(20) and all atomic/deterministic cuts), restrict Theorem thm - root_conv, thm - pdf_general and cor - mean_variance_gen accordingly, and delete the 'conditions are optimal' digression; recovering convergence for general cut densities would require a different (e.g. Perron–Frobenius/ergodic) argument without the explicit rate.
issues.overall_effect: The central Section 3 claim that any initial root distribution converges (uniformly, at rate $1-2\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$) to the uniform distribution for any cut distribution is unproven and false as stated; the asymptotic expected contraction factor for non-uniform priors (thm - pdf_general second part, cor - mean_variance_gen, the following Remark) and the abstract/introduction claims of full generality are unsupported. Only the uniform-prior results of Section 2 survive.
issues.title: Theorem thm - root_conv is false in general: the operator $\mathcal{T}$ is not positive on $B_\circ[0,1]$, so Gavrea–Ivan does not apply; deterministic cuts with a deterministic root give a counterexample
issues.why_classification: The main general result is false under its stated hypotheses and its proof rests on a misapplied theorem; any supported fix excludes an advertised regime (arbitrary cut distributions, in particular the near-bisection symmetric ones of principal interest) or requires essentially new proof architecture, and the dependent asymptotic rate results fall with it.

issues.failure_explanation: In the experiment the cuts are always $\mathcal{U}(0,1)$ and only the initial root distribution $\mathcal{R}$ varies. The rate $1-2(\mu-\mu^2-\sigma^2)$ in Theorem thm - root_conv is computed from the mean and variance of the cuts, so the theoretical value is $2/3$ for every column. The table instead lists $1-2\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$ evaluated with $c$ distributed as $\mathcal{R}$ (0.6, 0.7714, 0.9385, 0.5083), which is meaningless here. With the correct value $2/3$, the measured rates for Beta(0.5,2) (0.736) and Beta(0.1,2) (0.914) exceed the supposed 'upper bound', so the prose claim that asymmetric priors converge 'at a rate closer to the upper bound given by the theorem' and that symmetric ones beat it is not what the data show. The discrepancy is only explicable because the theorem's bound contains the floor $\varepsilon$ (which cannot be made small for priors with heavy mass near an endpoint), so the bound does not actually imply linear convergence at rate $1-2\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$, contrary to the surrounding prose and the Remark.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the 'Theoretical' row by $2/3$ for all columns, and rewrite the interpretation: explain that the bound of Theorem thm - root_conv includes the floor $\varepsilon$ governed by $|G_0(t)-t|$ near the endpoints, so it does not predict decay at rate $2/3$ for priors concentrated near an endpoint, and remove the statements that the convergence is linear with rate $1-2(\mu-\mu^2-\sigma^2)$ in general.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical validation of the convergence rate in Section 5.2 compares data to incorrect theoretical values, and the qualitative conclusions drawn (symmetric priors beat the theoretical rate, asymmetric priors approach it) are unsupported; the claim that the distribution of $r_n$ converges linearly at rate $1-2\mathbb{E}[c(1-c)]$ overstates what the bound gives.
